    Reproduction number and dispersion of secondary cases (superspreading)

    Source: R/outbreak-delays.R
    epi_offspring.Rd

    epi_offspring() fits a negative binomial offspring distribution to the number of secondary cases caused by each case (from contact tracing), estimating the reproduction number R and the dispersion k. Small k (below about 1) means transmission is concentrated in a few superspreaders (Lloyd-Smith et al. 2005). prop_80 is the proportion of cases expected to cause 80% of transmission (Endo et al. 2020).

    epi_chain_size() estimates the same two quantities from the final sizes of transmission chains (clusters), each started by one introduced case, using the chain-size distribution of Blumberg and Lloyd-Smith (2013). This needs R below 1 (chains that died out).

    Usage

    epi_offspring(.data, secondary, conf_level = 0.95)

epi_chain_size(.data, size, conf_level = 0.95)

    Arguments

    .data

    A data frame with one row per case (epi_offspring()) or per transmission chain (epi_chain_size()).

    secondary

    Number of secondary cases caused by each case.

    conf_level

    Confidence level (Wald intervals on the log scale).

    size

    Total number of cases in each chain, including the index case (1 or more).

    Value

    A one-row tibble with n, r, r_lower, r_upper, k, k_lower, k_upper, prop_80, p_zero (expected proportion of cases with no secondary cases), loglik and, for epi_offspring(), aic_poisson and aic_negbin (a smaller negative binomial AIC is evidence of overdispersion).

    References

    Lloyd-Smith, J. O., Schreiber, S. J., Kopp, P. E. and Getz, W. M. (2005). Superspreading and the effect of individual variation on disease emergence. Nature, 438, 355-359. doi:10.1038/nature04153

    Blumberg, S. and Lloyd-Smith, J. O. (2013). Inference of R0 and transmission heterogeneity from the size distribution of stuttering chains. PLOS Computational Biology, 9, e1002993. doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002993

    Endo, A., Abbott, S., Kucharski, A. J. and Funk, S. (2020). Estimating the overdispersion in COVID-19 transmission using outbreak sizes outside China. Wellcome Open Research, 5, 67. doi:10.12688/wellcomeopenres.15842.3

    Examples

    set.seed(3)
d <- data.frame(secondary = rnbinom(150, size = 0.3, mu = 1.2))
epi_offspring(d, secondary)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 12
#>       n     r r_lower r_upper     k k_lower k_upper prop_80 p_zero loglik
#>   <int> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1   150 0.967   0.722    1.29 0.434   0.274   0.688   0.292  0.601  -199.
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: aic_poisson <dbl>, aic_negbin <dbl>

chains <- data.frame(size = c(rep(1, 40), rep(2, 9), rep(3, 4), 5, 8, 21))
epi_chain_size(chains, size)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 10
#>       n     r r_lower r_upper     k k_lower k_upper prop_80 p_zero loglik
#>   <int> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    56 0.462   0.312   0.682 0.510   0.118    2.21   0.319  0.720  -60.4
